text:
A mean and a variance sum up one random variable. But the random variables you'll meet keep taking the same few shapes... and those shapes have names. Start with the smallest. One visitor either signs up or doesn't, with a chance of, say, point three. One yes or no is a Bernoulli trial. Now show the page to two hundred visitors, who each sign up with a chance of three in a hundred, and count the yeses. That count is binomial. Six is the likeliest number, and the chances fall away on either side. Ten or more? That happens about eight percent of the time. But it only holds if every visitor decides alone, with the same chance. A crowd sent by one TV ad, all behaving alike, makes the count swing far wider. And some counts have no fixed number of tries at all. Just a rate.

Say a help desk gets three tickets an hour, on average, each arriving on its own. The count in any one hour is Poisson. So how often does an hour bring eight or more, a spike worth staffing for? About one hour in eighty-four. Simulate a hundred thousand hours to check, and spikes come up one point one seven percent of the time. Close to the formula's one point one nine. A Poisson's mean and variance are the same number, here three. So if real counts vary far more than their average, events are clumping... and the Poisson will understate the spikes. One more kind of count is worth a name.

Count the tries until the first success. If each sales call closes one time in five, the calls until the first sale are geometric. On average, that's five calls. But the likeliest number is one... and eleven percent of the time, it takes more than ten.
